claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of PD pathology, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Familial cases of PD are often caused by mutations of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and the ubiquitin ligase Parkin.
source: Familial cases of PD are often caused by mutations of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and the ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both pivotal in maintaining mitochondrial quality control.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about familial PD genetics.

claim: PINK1 and Parkin are pivotal in maintaining mitochondrial quality control.
source: Familial cases of PD are often caused by mutations of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) and the ubiquitin ligase Parkin, both pivotal in maintaining mitochondrial quality control.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about PINK1 and Parkin function.

claim: CISD1 is a homodimeric mitochondrial iron-sulfur-binding protein.
source: CISD1, a homodimeric mitochondrial iron-sulfur-binding protein, is a major target of Parkin-mediated ubiquitination.
evidence: This is a known structural and functional characteristic of CISD1.

claim: CISD1 is a major target of Parkin-mediated ubiquitination.
source: CISD1, a homodimeric mitochondrial iron-sulfur-binding protein, is a major target of Parkin-mediated ubiquitination.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pink1 mutant flies exhibit a heightened propensity of CISD1 to form dimers.
source: We here discovered a heightened propensity of CISD1 to form dimers in Pink1 mutant flies and in dopaminergic neurons from PINK1 mutation patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons from PINK1 mutation patients exhibit a heightened propensity of CISD1 to form dimers.
source: We here discovered a heightened propensity of CISD1 to form dimers in Pink1 mutant flies and in dopaminergic neurons from PINK1 mutation patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The CISD1 dimer consists of two monomers that are covalently linked by a disulfide bridge.
source: The dimer consists of two monomers that are covalently linked by a disulfide bridge.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using reducing conditions and NEM treatment.

claim: CISD1 in the disulfide-bridged dimer conformation cannot coordinate the iron-sulfur cofactor.
source: In this conformation CISD1 cannot coordinate the iron-sulfur cofactor.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural requirement that the cysteines involved in the disulfide bond are the same ones that coordinate the Fe/S cluster.

claim: Overexpressing Cisd in Drosophila reduced climbing ability and lifespan.
source: Overexpressing Cisd, the Drosophila ortholog of CISD1, and a mutant Cisd incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster in Drosophila reduced climbing ability and lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fly assays.

claim: Overexpressing a mutant Cisd incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster in Drosophila reduced climbing ability and lifespan.
source: Overexpressing Cisd, the Drosophila ortholog of CISD1, and a mutant Cisd incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster in Drosophila reduced climbing ability and lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fly assays.

claim: The reduction in climbing ability and lifespan was more pronounced with mutant Cisd.
source: This was more pronounced with mutant Cisd and aggravated in Pink1 mutant flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing WT and mutant Cisd overexpression.

claim: The reduction in climbing ability and lifespan was aggravated in Pink1 mutant flies.
source: This was more pronounced with mutant Cisd and aggravated in Pink1 mutant flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Pink1 mutant flies.

claim: Complete loss of Cisd rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability.
source: Complete loss of Cisd, in contrast, rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability, wing posture, dopamine levels, lifespan, and mitochondrial ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout flies.

claim: Complete loss of Cisd rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on wing posture.
source: Complete loss of Cisd, in contrast, rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability, wing posture, dopamine levels, lifespan, and mitochondrial ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout flies.

claim: Complete loss of Cisd rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on dopamine levels.
source: Complete loss of Cisd, in contrast, rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability, wing posture, dopamine levels, lifespan, and mitochondrial ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout flies.

claim: Complete loss of Cisd rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on lifespan.
source: Complete loss of Cisd, in contrast, rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability, wing posture, dopamine levels, lifespan, and mitochondrial ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout flies.

claim: Complete loss of Cisd rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on mitochondrial ultrastructure.
source: Complete loss of Cisd, in contrast, rescued all detrimental effects of Pink1 mutation on climbing ability, wing posture, dopamine levels, lifespan, and mitochondrial ultrastructure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout flies.

claim: Iron-depleted Cisd operates downstream of Pink1.
source: Our results suggest that Cisd, probably iron-depleted Cisd, operates downstream of Pink1 shedding light on PD pathophysiology and implicating CISD1 as a potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments and the observation that Cisd loss rescues Pink1 phenotypes.

claim: CISD1 is implicated as a potential therapeutic target for PD.
source: Our results suggest that Cisd, probably iron-depleted Cisd, operates downstream of Pink1 shedding light on PD pathophysiology and implicating CISD1 as a potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: In healthy cells, PINK1 is continuously imported into mitochondria, where it is rapidly degraded.
source: In healthy cells, PINK1 is continuously imported into mitochondria, where it is rapidly degraded (Narendra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In unfit mitochondria with a reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, PINK1 import stalls.
source: However, in unfit mitochondria with a reduced mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm), PINK1 import stalls.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about PINK1 function.

claim: When PINK1 accumulates on damaged mitochondria, it phosphorylates various proteins, including the E3 ubiquitin ligase PRKN.
source: When PINK1 accumulates on damaged mitochondria, it phosphorylates various proteins, including the E3 ubiquitin ligase PRKN.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about PINK1/PRKN pathway.

claim: PINK1 phosphorylation activates PRKN, enabling it to attach ubiquitin to mitochondrial proteins.
source: This phosphorylation activates PRKN, enabling it to attach ubiquitin to mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about PINK1/PRKN pathway.

claim: Ubiquitination by PRKN acts as a signal for damaged mitochondria to be identified and engulfed by autophagosomes, initiating their degradation through mitophagy.
source: This ubiquitination acts as a signal for damaged mitochondria to be identified and engulfed by autophagosomes, initiating their degradation through mitophagy.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about mitophagy.

claim: Pink1 and Prkn loss of function in Drosophila melanogaster results in profound changes of the mitochondrial ultrastructure causing mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired flight and climbing ability, and a shortened lifespan.
source: Much of this mechanistic understanding has been elucidated in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster where Pink1 and Prkn loss of function results in profound changes of the mitochondrial ultrastructure causing mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired flight and climbing ability, and a shortened lifespan (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PD patients exhibit elevated iron levels within the substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: PD patients exhibit elevated iron levels within the substantia nigra pars compacta, and this iron accumulation correlates with the severity of the disease (Dexter et al., 1987; Hirsch et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Iron accumulation in the substantia nigra pars compacta correlates with the severity of PD.
source: PD patients exhibit elevated iron levels within the substantia nigra pars compacta, and this iron accumulation correlates with the severity of the disease (Dexter et al., 1987; Hirsch et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Iron dysregulation is apparent even in asymptomatic carriers of PRKN mutations.
source: Notably, this iron dysregulation is apparent even in asymptomatic carriers of PRKN mutations (Pyatigorskaya et al., 2015), suggesting that it is an early event and correlates with mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Iron dysregulation is an early event in PD and correlates with mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Notably, this iron dysregulation is apparent even in asymptomatic carriers of PRKN mutations (Pyatigorskaya et al., 2015), suggesting that it is an early event and correlates with mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation in asymptomatic carriers.

claim: Human dopaminergic neurons lacking PINK1 display inhibition of the iron-dependent mitochondrial aconitase.
source: Furthermore, human dopaminergic neurons lacking PINK1 display inhibition of the iron-dependent mitochondrial aconitase, leading to accumulation of NAD+ and depletion of essential metabolites (Bus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial aconitase in PINK1-lacking neurons leads to accumulation of NAD+ and depletion of essential metabolites.
source: Furthermore, human dopaminergic neurons lacking PINK1 display inhibition of the iron-dependent mitochondrial aconitase, leading to accumulation of NAD+ and depletion of essential metabolites (Bus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Pink1 deficiency in flies results in inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase by impairing its labile iron-sulfur cluster.
source: In flies, Pink1 deficiency similarly results in inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase by impairing its labile iron-sulfur cluster, leading to oxidative distress and mitochondrial swelling (Esposito et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase in Pink1-deficient flies leads to oxidative distress and mitochondrial swelling.
source: In flies, Pink1 deficiency similarly results in inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase by impairing its labile iron-sulfur cluster, leading to oxidative distress and mitochondrial swelling (Esposito et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CISD1 is also known as mitoNEET.
source: An important target protein of PINK1/PRKN crucial for iron homeostasis and redox homeostasis is CISD1, also known as mitoNEET (reviewed in Mittler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: CISD1 is crucial for iron homeostasis and redox homeostasis.
source: An important target protein of PINK1/PRKN crucial for iron homeostasis and redox homeostasis is CISD1, also known as mitoNEET (reviewed in Mittler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: CISD1 is a homodimeric protein N-terminally inserted into the outer mitochondrial membrane facing the cytosol.
source: CISD1 is a homodimeric protein N-terminally inserted into the outer mitochondrial membrane facing the cytosol (Wiley et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CISD1 is ubiquitinated by PRKN.
source: CISD1 is ubiquitinated by PRKN (Sarraf et al., 2013) and its levels are reduced upon dissipation of Δψm (Chan et al., 2011; Cunningham et al., 2015; Lazarou et al., 2013; McWilliams et al., 2018; Narendra et al., 2012; Okatsu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CISD1 levels are reduced upon dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: CISD1 is ubiquitinated by PRKN (Sarraf et al., 2013) and its levels are reduced upon dissipation of Δψm (Chan et al., 2011; Cunningham et al., 2015; Lazarou et al., 2013; McWilliams et al., 2018; Narendra et al., 2012; Okatsu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CISD1 forms a complex with PRKN.
source: Moreover, CISD1 forms a complex with PRKN, and this interaction is markedly increased by activation of PINK1 and ubiquitination (Narendra et al., 2013; Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The interaction between CISD1 and PRKN is markedly increased by activation of PINK1 and ubiquitination.
source: Moreover, CISD1 forms a complex with PRKN, and this interaction is markedly increased by activation of PINK1 and ubiquitination (Narendra et al., 2013; Sarraf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, the homolog of CISD1 is the most strongly ubiquitinated protein in response to Prkn overexpression in vivo.
source: In Drosophila, the homolog of CISD1 is the most strongly ubiquitinated protein in response to Prkn overexpression in vivo (Martinez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each monomer of CISD1 harbors a 2Fe/2S cluster coordinated by three cysteines (Cys72,74,83) and one histidine (His87).
source: Functionally, CISD1 exists as a homodimer, and each monomer of CISD1 harbors an 2Fe/2S (2 iron/2 sulfur) cluster coordinated by three cysteines (Cys72,74,83) and one histidine (His87).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about CISD1 structure.

claim: Most conventional 2Fe/2S clusters are coordinated by four cysteines or two cysteines and two histidines.
source: In contrast, most conventional 2Fe/2S clusters are coordinated by four cysteines or two cysteines and two histidines (Wiley et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The unconventional coordination of the CISD1 2Fe/2S cluster renders it more susceptible to oxidation.
source: This peculiarity renders the CISD1 2Fe/2S cluster more susceptible to oxidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural difference in coordination.

claim: The transfer of the iron-sulfur cluster from CISD1 to stress-sensitive Fe/S proteins constitutes a cellular adaptive response that helps recovery from oxidative injury.
source: It was thus proposed that the transfer of the iron-sulfur cluster from CISD1 to stress-sensitive Fe/S proteins constitutes a cellular adaptive response that helps recovery from oxidative injury (reviewed in Mittler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The oxidized 2Fe/2S cluster of CISD1 can be transferred to iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP1).
source: In support of this hypothesis, it has been demonstrated that the oxidized 2Fe/2S cluster of CISD1 can be transferred to iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP1) (Ferecatu et al., 2014), a bifunctional protein that can switch between two distinct enzymatic activities based on the availability of iron.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When iron levels are sufficient, IRP1 binds a 2Fe/2S cluster, converting it into a functional aconitase enzyme.
source: When iron levels are sufficient, IRP1 binds an 2Fe/2S cluster, converting it into a functional aconitase enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about IRP1 function.

claim: When iron levels are low, IRP1 loses its 2Fe/2S cluster and undergoes a conformational change to function as an RNA-binding protein.
source: When iron levels are low, IRP1 loses its 2Fe/2S cluster and undergoes a conformational change. In this state, known as the 'apo' form, IRP1 functions as an RNA-binding protein and binds to specific RNA sequences called iron-responsive elements (IREs) located in the untranslated regions of target mRNAs (reviewed by Rouault and Maio, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: CISD1 is capable of recycling the cytosolic apo-IRP1 to holo-aconitase by donating its 2Fe/2S cluster.
source: CISD1 is capable of recycling the cytosolic apo-IRP1 to holo-aconitase by donating its 2Fe/2S cluster (Camponeschi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cardiac myocytes from Cisd1 knockout mice exhibit a reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
source: Cardiac myocytes from Cisd1 knockout (KO) mice exhibit a reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Wiley et al., 2007a), akin to KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) where this dysfunction is attributed to a reduction in the total cellular mitochondrial volume (Vernay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cisd1 KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibit reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity attributed to a reduction in the total cellular mitochondrial volume.
source: Cardiac myocytes from Cisd1 knockout (KO) mice exhibit a reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity (Wiley et al., 2007a), akin to KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) where this dysfunction is attributed to a reduction in the total cellular mitochondrial volume (Vernay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, there is a single ortholog of CISD1 initially named Cisd2.
source: In Drosophila, there is a single ortholog of CISD1 initially named Cisd2 because it is slightly more similar to the mammalian CISD2 than to CISD1 (Jones et al., 2014) protein.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human CISD2 is located at the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Human CISD2 is located at the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Overexpression of Cisd2 in fly muscles is detrimental and results in mitochondrial enlargement and the formation of double-membraned vesicles containing cytosolic proteins within mitochondria.
source: Overexpression of Cisd2 (this publication used the alternative name Dosmit) in fly muscles is detrimental and results in mitochondrial enlargement and the formation of double-membraned vesicles containing cytosolic proteins within mitochondria (Chen et al., 2020), implicating Cisd2 in the regulation of mitochondrial morphology.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fly Cisd2 is an Fe/S protein and all amino acids linked to cluster coordination are conserved.
source: Similar to human CISD1, fly Cisd2 is an Fe/S protein and all amino acids linked to cluster coordination are conserved.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about protein conservation.

claim: Fly Cisd2 interacts with IRP1.
source: In addition, fly Cisd2 (this publication used the alternative name MitoNEET) interacts with IRP1 (Huynh et al., 2019) further linking Cisd2 to iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PINK1 Q456X neurons expressed diminished PINK1 mRNA levels.
source: Notably, PINK1 Q456X neurons expressed diminished PINK1 mRNA levels (Figure 1A) and reduced levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (as depicted in exemplary blots from our differentiations in Figure 1B, with quantification of different independent differentiations reported in Jarazo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PINK1 Q456X neurons expressed reduced levels of tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: Notably, PINK1 Q456X neurons expressed diminished PINK1 mRNA levels (Figure 1A) and reduced levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (as depicted in exemplary blots from our differentiations in Figure 1B, with quantification of different independent differentiations reported in Jarazo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in a cited paper.

claim: PINK1 Q456X dopaminergic neurons exhibit an increased CISD1 dimer/monomer ratio compared to gene-corrected controls.
source: When pooled together, this analysis revealed a significant increase in CISD1 dimerization in mutant PINK1 neurons compared to gene-corrected controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CISD1 C83S, the mutant incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster, exhibits a significant increase in dimerization.
source: By comparing the dimerization patterns of the CISD1 variants, we observed a significant increase in dimerization for C83S CISD1, the mutant incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by split luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Iron-depleted CISD1 has a higher propensity for dimerization.
source: This finding suggested that iron-depleted CISD1 has a higher propensity for dimerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the C83S mutant data.

claim: In silico analysis revealed a larger surface-surface contact between the C83S monomers, indicating a closer binding compared to WT CISD1.
source: This analysis unveiled a larger surface-surface contact between the C83S monomers, indicating a closer binding compared to WT CISD1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Iron chelation with deferiprone resulted in increased CISD1 dimerization.
source: Remarkably, our results demonstrated that under these conditions only iron chelation resulted in increased dimerization (Figure 2C) that mirrored the increased dimerization seen in the C83S mutant, which is unable to coordinate the 2Fe/2S complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by split luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Treatment with FCCP did not result in increased CISD1 dimerization.
source: Remarkably, our results demonstrated that under these conditions only iron chelation resulted in increased dimerization (Figure 2C) that mirrored the increased dimerization seen in the C83S mutant, which is unable to coordinate the 2Fe/2S complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the statement that 'only iron chelation' resulted in increased dimerization, implying other treatments did not.

claim: Treatment with antimycin/oligomycin did not result in increased CISD1 dimerization.
source: Remarkably, our results demonstrated that under these conditions only iron chelation resulted in increased dimerization (Figure 2C) that mirrored the increased dimerization seen in the C83S mutant, which is unable to coordinate the 2Fe/2S complex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the statement that 'only iron chelation' resulted in increased dimerization, implying other treatments did not.

claim: WT MEF cells treated with deferiprone showed increased CISD1 dimer formation and the presence of a CISD1 multimer.
source: To corroborate this, we expanded our analysis to WT MEF cells treated with deferiprone. Immunoblotting revealed increased dimer formation and even the presence of a CISD1 multimer under these conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increased dimer formation in PINK1 mutant neurons likely represents the presence of apo-CISD1, a form of CISD1 devoid of its iron-sulfur cluster.
source: Consequently, we conclude that the increased dimer formation in the PINK1 mutant neurons likely represents the presence of apo-CISD1, a form of CISD1 devoid of its iron-sulfur cluster, and that this is caused by changes in the iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the deferiprone and C83S mutant experiments.

claim: The increased dimer formation in PINK1 mutant neurons is caused by changes in iron homeostasis.
source: Consequently, we conclude that the increased dimer formation in the PINK1 mutant neurons likely represents the presence of apo-CISD1, a form of CISD1 devoid of its iron-sulfur cluster, and that this is caused by changes in the iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the deferiprone experiments.

claim: Pink1B9 flies have a large deletion of the coding region and almost no remaining mRNA expression.
source: Pink1B9 flies (Park et al., 2006) are on the w1118 background and have a large deletion of the coding region and almost no remaining mRNA expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PCR and qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no changes in Cisd mRNA levels in Pink1B9 flies.
source: At the mRNA level, we observed no changes in Cisd mRNA levels in Pink1B9 flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fly Cisd runs as a monomer and dimer even on reducing gels containing dithiothreitol.
source: We then immunoblotted samples from young (3-day-old) and old (8-week-old) WT w1118 and Pink1B9 flies and noted that fly Cisd, similar to mouse CISD1, runs as a monomer and dimer even on reducing gels containing dithiothreitol (DTT) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Young Pink1 mutant flies have reduced total Cisd protein levels compared to WT flies.
source: This analysis unveiled reduced total Cisd protein levels in young Pink1 mutant flies compared to WT flies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Old Pink1B9 flies exhibit a significant increase in Cisd dimer/monomer ratio compared to young Pink1B9 flies and to old WT flies.
source: When assessing the dimer/monomer ratio, we observed a significant increase in dimer levels in old Pink1B9 flies compared to young Pink1B9 flies and to old WT flies (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Age had no effect on dimerization of WT flies.
source: Age had no effect on dimerization of WT flies (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Prolonged incubation with higher concentrations of DTT and TCEP followed by boiling resulted in the loss of dimeric and an increase of monomeric Cisd.
source: To elucidate the nature of the dimer, we next used extremely reducing conditions of prolonged incubation with higher concentrations of DTT and tris-(2-carboxyethyl)-phosphine as a disulfide-bond breaking agent followed by boiling. This resulted in the loss of dimeric and an increase of monomeric Cisd (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increased dimer formation was observed in old Pink1B9 flies under non-reducing conditions with NEM treatment.
source: We also added the thiol alkylating agent N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) during lysis and performed non-reducing immunoblotting in old Pink1B9 flies compared to old WT flies. NEM blocks all reduced sulfhydryl (-SH) groups of cysteine residues and thereby prevents the formation of disulfide bonds due to non-specific oxidation during the lysis process (Figure 3F). We also observed the increased dimer formation in old Pink1B9 flies under these conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The increased dimerization in old Pink1B9 flies is most probably caused by the formation of an intermolecular disulfide linking two Cisd molecules.
source: Together these experiments indicate that the increased dimerization in old Pink1B9 flies is most probably caused by the formation of an intermolecular disulfide linking two Cisd molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the reducing conditions and NEM experiments.

claim: Pink1 mutant flies have a heightened total iron content.
source: This revealed a heightened total iron content in Pink1 mutants (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Pink1 mutant flies have an enrichment of redox-active Fe2+ ions compared to redox-inactive Fe3+.
source: Delving deeper with capillary electrophoresis-inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (CE-ICP-MS), we then identified an enrichment of redox-active Fe2+ ions in these mutants compared to the more subdued presence of redox-inactive Fe3+ (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by CE-ICP-MS data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Pink1B9 flies are in a more pro-oxidative state.
source: In the Fenton reaction, ferrous iron (Fe2+) forms hydroxyl radicals (•OH), a highly reactive and destructive free radical, and ferric iron (Fe3+) in the presence of hydrogen peroxide. Pink1B9 flies are therefore in a more pro-oxidative state.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio.

claim: Pink1B9 flies are dramatically more susceptible to iron depletion with deferiprone.
source: Pink1B9 flies were also dramatically more susceptible to iron depletion with deferiprone. In these experiments, we fed developing WT and Pink1 mutant flies food supplemented with 65 µM deferiprone, a concentration that did not induce widespread mitophagy in Pink1B9 flies (Lee et al., 2018), and quantified the number of adult flies eclosing from pupae. This revealed that iron depletion also showed a trend toward reduced eclosion of WT flies but nearly completely abrogated the eclosion of Pink1 mutant flies (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ubiquitous overexpression of Cisd and apo-Cisd aggravated reduced climbing speed and lifespan in WT and Pink1 mutant flies.
source: Ubiquitous overexpression of Cisd and apo-Cisd aggravated these phenotypes in WT and Pink1 mutant flies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by climbing and lifespan data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cisd C/S overexpression was associated with a more profound reduction in climbing speed compared to WT Cisd.
source: Cisd C/S overexpression was, however, associated with a more profound reduction in climbing speed compared to WT Cisd, while the effects on lifespan were similarly detrimental (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The vast majority of all Cisd C/S-overexpressing flies were not capable of inflating their wings.
source: Additionally, the vast majority of all Cisd C/S-overexpressing flies were not capable of inflating their wings (Figure 4B), a rather non-specific phenotype which can result from genetic mutations, environmental conditions, and developmental defects.
evidence: This is supported by wing phenotype data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Newly eclosed flies expressing C/S Cisd displayed significantly higher levels of GstS1 mRNA in w1118.
source: Interestingly, newly eclosed flies expressing C/S Cisd displayed significantly higher levels of GstS1 mRNA in w1118 in line with a compensatory increase in the defense against oxidative distress induced by apo-Cisd (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pink1B9 flies were not capable of raising the GstS1 antioxidant defense in response to apo-Cisd expression.
source: Pink1B9 flies, in contrast, were not capable of raising this antioxidant defense in response to apo-Cisd expression (Figure 4C) which might explain part of the additional toxic effect.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of Cisd led to an approximately 60% reduction of Cisd protein levels.
source: Knockdown of Cisd led to an approximately 60% reduction of Cisd protein levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Knockdown of Cisd effectively rescued the reduced lifespan of Pink1 mutant males.
source: Importantly, this knockdown effectively rescued the reduced lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) of Pink1 mutant males, suggesting a detrimental effect of Cisd in flies lacking Pink1.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Flies devoid of Cisd protein expression exhibited no discernible difference in climbing ability up to 30 days of age.
source: Flies devoid of Cisd protein expression exhibited no discernible difference in climbing ability up to 30 days of age (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) and only a minor reduction in lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cisd KO flies have only a minor reduction in lifespan.
source: Flies devoid of Cisd protein expression exhibited no discernible difference in climbing ability up to 30 days of age (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B) and only a minor reduction in lifespan (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Cisd runs as a monomer, a dimer, and a weak multimer.
source: The complete KO allowed us to observe that Cisd not only runs as a monomer (M), a dimer (D) as shown and quantified earlier, but also as a weak multimer (X) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pink1 mRNA levels were reduced in Pink1B9 flies.
source: Pink1 levels were reduced in Pink1B9 but unchanged in Cisd KO flies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pink1 mRNA levels were unchanged in Cisd KO flies.
source: Pink1 levels were reduced in Pink1B9 but unchanged in Cisd KO flies (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pink1B9 flies exhibited reduced climbing ability.
source: As expected, Pink1B9 flies exhibited reduced climbing ability (Figure 5C), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 5D), a decreased lifespan (Figure 5E), and diminished dopamine levels (Figure 5F) in line with prior reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pink1B9 flies exhibited an abnormal wing posture.
source: As expected, Pink1B9 flies exhibited reduced climbing ability (Figure 5C), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 5D), a decreased lifespan (Figure 5E), and diminished dopamine levels (Figure 5F) in line with prior reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by wing posture data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pink1B9 flies exhibited a decreased lifespan.
source: As expected, Pink1B9 flies exhibited reduced climbing ability (Figure 5C), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 5D), a decreased lifespan (Figure 5E), and diminished dopamine levels (Figure 5F) in line with prior reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pink1B9 flies exhibited diminished dopamine levels.
source: As expected, Pink1B9 flies exhibited reduced climbing ability (Figure 5C), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 5D), a decreased lifespan (Figure 5E), and diminished dopamine levels (Figure 5F) in line with prior reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by dopamine quantification shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Double-knockout flies lacking both Cisd and Pink1 exhibited normal climbing ability.
source: Remarkably, when compared to Pink1B9 flies these DKO exhibited normal climbing ability, normal wing morphology, normal dopamine levels, and a normal lifespan, essentially representing a complete rescue of these phenotypes (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Double-knockout flies lacking both Cisd and Pink1 exhibited normal wing morphology.
source: Remarkably, when compared to Pink1B9 flies these DKO exhibited normal climbing ability, normal wing morphology, normal dopamine levels, and a normal lifespan, essentially representing a complete rescue of these phenotypes (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by wing posture data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Double-knockout flies lacking both Cisd and Pink1 exhibited normal dopamine levels.
source: Remarkably, when compared to Pink1B9 flies these DKO exhibited normal climbing ability, normal wing morphology, normal dopamine levels, and a normal lifespan, essentially representing a complete rescue of these phenotypes (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by dopamine quantification shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Double-knockout flies lacking both Cisd and Pink1 exhibited a normal lifespan.
source: Remarkably, when compared to Pink1B9 flies these DKO exhibited normal climbing ability, normal wing morphology, normal dopamine levels, and a normal lifespan, essentially representing a complete rescue of these phenotypes (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In Pink1B9 flies, flight muscles are atrophied and mitochondria cover less space, are smaller, and have a significantly reduced number of cristae resulting in a reduction of cristae surface.
source: In Pink1B9 flies, flight muscles are atrophied and mitochondria cover less space, are smaller, and have a significantly reduced number of cristae resulting in a reduction of cristae surface (Figure 5G, a comparison of all four genotypes is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Concurrent Cisd KO effectively rescued all mitochondrial and cristae morphology phenotypes in Pink1B9 flies.
source: Intriguingly, the concurrent Cisd KO effectively rescued all these phenotypes (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cisd mRNA was dramatically reduced in Prkn mutant flies.
source: As expected, Park25 flies expressed no Prkn mRNA, but, intriguingly, Cisd mRNA was also dramatically reduced in Prkn mutant flies (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Prkn mRNA was nearly undetectable in Cisd KO flies.
source: Similarly, Prkn mRNA was nearly undetectable in Cisd KO flies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Total Cisd protein levels were downregulated in both young and old Prkn mutant flies.
source: When we examined total Cisd protein levels, we observed a downregulation of total Cisd levels in both young and old Prkn mutant flies in line with the mRNA results (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Cisd dimer/monomer ratio was unchanged in Prkn mutant flies.
source: The dimer/monomer ratio was unchanged and displayed again a considerable degree of variability (Figure 6D, D').
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot quantification shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Park25 flies exhibited a notable reduction in climbing ability.
source: Like Pink1B9 flies, Park25 flies exhibited a notable reduction in climbing ability (Figure 6E), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 6F), and a shortened lifespan (Figure 6G), consistent with previous reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Park25 flies exhibited an abnormal wing posture.
source: Like Pink1B9 flies, Park25 flies exhibited a notable reduction in climbing ability (Figure 6E), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 6F), and a shortened lifespan (Figure 6G), consistent with previous reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by wing posture data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Park25 flies exhibited a shortened lifespan.
source: Like Pink1B9 flies, Park25 flies exhibited a notable reduction in climbing ability (Figure 6E), an abnormal wing posture (Figure 6F), and a shortened lifespan (Figure 6G), consistent with previous reports (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Concurrent Cisd KO conferred complete protection against the climbing impairment of Park25 flies.
source: Intriguingly, concurrent Cisd KO conferred complete protection against the climbing impairment of Park25 flies (Figure 6E) and showed a distinct inclination toward normal wing posture with DKO being not significantly different from WT flies (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by climbing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Concurrent Cisd KO showed a distinct inclination toward normal wing posture in Park25 flies.
source: Intriguingly, concurrent Cisd KO conferred complete protection against the climbing impairment of Park25 flies (Figure 6E) and showed a distinct inclination toward normal wing posture with DKO being not significantly different from WT flies (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by wing posture data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Cisd/Prkn double-knockout did not rescue the lifespan of Park25 flies.
source: However, surprisingly, DKO did not rescue the lifespan of Park25 flies (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cisd likely serves an essential, yet undiscovered, function, particularly in the aging fly, and its loss is compensated for in the presence of Prkn.
source: This observation suggests that Cisd likely serves an essential, yet undiscovered, function, particularly in the aging fly, and its loss is compensated for in the presence of Prkn.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue effects in Pink1 vs Prkn mutants.

claim: The slower-migrating form of CISD1/Cisd likely does not represent a ubiquitinated form.
source: The slower-migrating form likely does not represent a ubiquitinated form, as treatment with the deubiquitinase USP2 had no effect on fly Cisd dimerization (Martinez et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Under non-reducing conditions, recombinant CISD1 ran as a monomeric and a dimeric band while under reducing conditions using beta-mercaptoethanol only the monomeric band was detected.
source: Under non-reducing conditions, recombinant CISD1 ran as a monomeric and a dimeric band while under reducing conditions using beta-mercaptoethanol only the monomeric band was detected (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The disulfide bond in CISD1 forms between cysteine C83 and either C72 or C74.
source: Using proteomic analysis, it was determined that the disulfide bond forms between cysteine C83 and either C72 or C74 of CISD1 (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Formation of the disulfide bond in CISD1 results in loss of the Fe/S cluster because the residues involved in bond formation also coordinate the Fe/S cluster.
source: Formation of the disulfide bond therefore results in loss of the Fe/S cluster because the residues involved in bond formation also coordinate the Fe/S cluster of CISD1.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural requirement that the same cysteines are involved in both processes.

claim: CISD1 C83S is probably incapable of forming a disulfide bond.
source: However, CISD1 C83S, a genetically engineered CISD1 incapable of binding the iron-sulfur cluster and probably also incapable of forming a disulfide bond (Roberts et al., 2013), has a higher propensity for dimer formation when analyzed in a cellular assay based on complementation of split luciferase (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fe/S cluster loss comes first and results in an altered structure that facilitates the formation of the disulfide bond.
source: This suggests that Fe/S cluster loss comes first and results in an altered structure that facilitates the formation of the disulfide bond.
evidence: This is inferred from the C83S mutant data showing increased dimerization despite inability to form disulfide bonds.

claim: CISD1 can receive its Fe/S cluster from its homolog CISD3 in the mitochondrial matrix via the porin VDAC1.
source: A recent report suggested that CISD1 can receive its Fe/S cluster from its homolog CISD3 (aka MiNT) in the mitochondrial matrix via the porin VDAC1 (Karmi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The apo-CISD1/Cisd observed in PINK1 mutant dopaminergic neurons and Pink1 mutant flies may constitute a permanently fixed apo-CISD1/Cisd that cannot be reconstituted.
source: So it appears possible that either this transfer is inhibited/attenuated or that the apo-CISD1/Cisd observed in PINK1 mutant dopaminergic neurons and Pink1 mutant flies constitutes a permanently fixed apo-CISD1/Cisd that cannot be reconstituted.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed accumulation of apo-CISD1.

claim: Knockdown of CISD1 in cells significantly reduces the cytosolic aconitase activity.
source: Knockdown of CISD1 in cells indeed significantly reduces the cytosolic aconitase activity (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Apo-IRP1 binds to IREs in the mRNA of iron-responsive genes.
source: On the other hand, apo-IRP1 not only lacks aconitase activity but also binds to IREs in the mRNA of iron-responsive genes (Haile et al., 1992a; Haile et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Association of apo-IRP1 with IREs in the 5' untranslated region of ferritin mRNA inhibits ferritin translation resulting in less bound iron and an increase in free iron.
source: Association with IREs in the 5' untranslated region of ferritin mRNA inhibits ferritin translation resulting in less bound iron and an increase in free iron (Chen et al., 1997) while association with IREs in the 3' untranslated region of the mRNA encoding the iron importers transferrin receptor 1 and SLC11A2 stabilizes the mRNAs and facilitates their translation resulting in increased iron import (Galy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Association of apo-IRP1 with IREs in the 3' untranslated region of the mRNA encoding the iron importers transferrin receptor 1 and SLC11A2 stabilizes the mRNAs and facilitates their translation resulting in increased iron import.
source: Association with IREs in the 5' untranslated region of ferritin mRNA inhibits ferritin translation resulting in less bound iron and an increase in free iron (Chen et al., 1997) while association with IREs in the 3' untranslated region of the mRNA encoding the iron importers transferrin receptor 1 and SLC11A2 stabilizes the mRNAs and facilitates their translation resulting in increased iron import (Galy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The transcriptional changes caused by the presence of apo-IRP1 result in iron overload.
source: Together the transcriptional changes caused by the presence of apo-IRP1 result in iron overload which is an important factor in the pathology associated with PD (recently reviewed in Ma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of apo-IRP1 on iron metabolism genes and supported by a citation.

claim: KO of PINK1 in flies results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
source: Notably, KO of PINK1 in flies (Esposito et al., 2013), in mice (Gautier et al., 2008), and in human dopaminergic neurons (Bus et al., 2020) also results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: KO of PINK1 in mice results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
source: Notably, KO of PINK1 in flies (Esposito et al., 2013), in mice (Gautier et al., 2008), and in human dopaminergic neurons (Bus et al., 2020) also results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: KO of PINK1 in human dopaminergic neurons results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
source: Notably, KO of PINK1 in flies (Esposito et al., 2013), in mice (Gautier et al., 2008), and in human dopaminergic neurons (Bus et al., 2020) also results in a reduced aconitase activity in mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial aconitase contains an IRE in its 5' untranslated region, making its expression subject to repression by apo-IRP1.
source: Mitochondrial aconitase contains an IRE in its 5' untranslated region (Kim et al., 1996), making its expression subject to repression by apo-IRP1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and inferred from the known function of apo-IRP1.

claim: The inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase caused by Pink1 loss of function triggers increased superoxide production, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial swelling.
source: The inactivation of mitochondrial aconitase caused by Pink1 loss of function triggers increased superoxide production, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial swelling (Esposito et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Overexpression of mitoferrin mitigates the reduced mitochondrial aconitase activity, abnormal wing posture, flight deficits, and mitochondrial morphology defects associated with Pink1 loss of function by elevating mitochondrial bioavailable iron levels.
source: Others reproduced these findings and reported that overexpression of mitoferrin, a mitochondrial iron transporter, mitigates the reduced mitochondrial aconitase activity, abnormal wing posture, flight deficits, and mitochondrial morphology defects associated with Pink1 loss of function by elevating mitochondrial bioavailable iron levels (Wan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: KO of IRP2 results in iron accumulation and Parkinsonism in mice.
source: Interestingly, KO of IRP2, a protein highly homologous to IRP1 but lacking aconitase activity, results in iron accumulation and Parkinsonism in mice (LaVaute et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The accumulation of apo-CISD1/Cisd and the subsequent inability to repair defective IRP1/2 would place CISD1 upstream of the changes in iron homeostasis observed in PD and models of PD.
source: The accumulation of apo-CISD1/Cisd and the subsequent inability to repair defective IRP1/2 would place CISD1 upstream of the changes in iron homeostasis observed in PD and models of PD (Ma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: Prolonged exposure of MEFs to the iron-depleting agent 2,2′-bipyridine results in downregulation of Cisd1.
source: Interestingly, prolonged exposure of MEFs to the iron-depleting agent 2,2′-bipyridine results in downregulation of Cisd1 (Key et al., 2020) possibly as a compensatory mechanism to limit the abundance of such a toxic iron-depleted CISD1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of Cisd in muscle decreased the lifespan of flies and resulted in enlarged mitochondria containing numerous intramitochondrial vesicles surrounded by a double membrane.
source: Previous work demonstrated that ectopic overexpression of Cisd in muscle decreased the lifespan of flies and resulted in enlarged mitochondria containing numerous intramitochondrial vesicles surrounded by a double membrane (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Both genetic and pharmacological suppression of CISD1 and Cisd restored increased calcium release from the ER conferred by PINK1 and Parkin mutation in mammalian cells and flies.
source: Very recent work, published during the revision of this manuscript, discovered that both genetic and pharmacological suppression of CISD1 and Cisd restored increased calcium release from the ER conferred by PINK1 and Parkin mutation in mammalian cells and flies (Ham et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cisd depletion using RNAi protects against Pink1 and Prkn loss of function in flies.
source: Also Martinez et al. very recently reported that Cisd depletion using RNAi protects against Pink1 and Prkn loss of function in flies (Martinez et al., 2024), suggesting that a reduction, instead of a complete KO, of Cisd as used by us is more beneficial in Park25 flies and equally beneficial in Pink1B9 flies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cisd levels increased in Pink1 and Prkn mutant flies according to Martinez et al.
source: In their hands, Cisd levels increased in Pink1 and Prkn mutant flies which was not evident in our study.
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from another study.

claim: Cisd overexpression was neurotoxic, disrupted mitochondrial morphology, and led to an accumulation of phospho-ubiquitin.
source: Cisd overexpression was neurotoxic, disrupted mitochondrial morphology, and led to an accumulation of phospho-ubiquitin which they speculate also blocks mitophagy, resulting in the accumulation of more defective mitochondria (Martinez et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster protein Cisd is downstream of the pathophysiological cascade initiated by Pink1 and partially Prkn loss of function in flies and probably also in humans.
source: In summary, our results suggest that the mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster protein Cisd is downstream of the pathophysiological cascade initiated by Pink1 and partially Prkn loss of function in flies and probably also in humans.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental findings.
